title: Potato Gnocchi
subtitle: Soft pillowy potato dumplings
excerpt: The Italian dumpling that requires no equipment beyond your hands: floury potatoes riced while still hot, worked with egg and flour into a soft dough, cut into pillows, and cooked in salted water until they float. Light when made with care; stodgy when not.

recipe.sourceNotes: Potato gnocchi (the word gnocchi means lumps or knuckles) became widespread across northern Italy in the late nineteenth century, after the potato was fully adopted into Italian peasant cooking. They exist in many forms across the peninsula: northern versions tend to use more flour and are firmer; Venetian versions use less flour and more potato for a lighter result. The critical variable is potato type: floury, low-moisture potatoes such as King Edward or Maris Piper are essential. Waxy potatoes release too much moisture, absorb more flour, and produce heavy gnocchi. The second critical factor is to work the dough as little as possible once the flour is added: overworking develops gluten and makes the gnocchi tough. The classic test is to cook one gnocco first to check the texture; if it falls apart, add a little more flour. If it is heavy and leaden, the potatoes were the wrong type or were too wet.

content.text: Bake or boil the potatoes in their skins: the skin prevents them absorbing water, which is the enemy of light gnocchi. Rice them while still hot; hot potato absorbs less flour. Use the minimum flour that allows the dough to hold together. Test one gnocco in boiling water before cutting the rest.

items.preparation: large, floury potatoes such as Maris Piper or King Edward; baked or boiled in their skins

content.text: While the potatoes are still hot, scoop out the flesh and pass through a potato ricer onto a lightly floured work surface. Spread the riced potato out and leave to cool for 5 minutes; this allows steam to escape. Make a well in the centre and add the egg, salt, and parmesan if using.

Add 100 g of the flour and bring together with your hands, working quickly and lightly until a soft, slightly sticky dough forms. Add more flour a tablespoon at a time only if the dough is too sticky to handle; it should be soft and just dry enough to roll.

Divide the dough into 6 pieces. Roll each into a rope about 1.5 cm thick on a floured surface. Cut across into 2 cm pieces. Cook in batches in well-salted boiling water: they are done about 30 seconds after they float to the surface. Lift out with a slotted spoon. Serve immediately with butter and sage, or with a simple tomato sauce.
